abstract: Mechanical changes are increasingly recognised as an integral component of tumour response to therapy and can be effectively used as a tumour biomarker in designing and testing new anticancer therapies. Assessing these changes in situ in a live tumour model, however, without disturbing cellular function, remains a challenge. We investigated dose-dependent responses to anticancer drugs in live three-dimensional triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) spheroids using label-free Brillouin microscopy, complemented by bulk compression testing and biological assays. Increasing drug concentration produced a progressive reduction in apparent stiffness of the tumour spheroids, accompanied by a reduction in Brillouin frequency shift, indicating treatment-associated mechanical softening of spheroids. These mechanical responses were accompanied by drug-dependent changes in cell cycle-associated signals and membrane-integrity markers. Spatially resolved Brillouin mapping revealed the heterogeneous distribution of spheroid mechanical properties. The combined approach based on bulk spheroid compression and microscale Brillouin mapping provides an integrated dual-scale view of treatment-associated mechanics in live tumour models. Importantly, Brillouin microscopy detected spectral changes in conditions where the relative metabolic activity of intact spheroids remained statistically unchanged. Together, these findings highlight the potential of Brillouin microscopy for detecting early responses to anticancer drugs, supporting a greater focus on individualised approaches to monitoring tumour response.
